phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'say'; Old Norse initial s is plain and unaspirated.
Short close front rounded vowel [y] — the tongue arched forward as for English 'ee' while the lips stay rounded as for 'oo'; the vowel of French tu and German über, written with the plain letter y.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], as in English 'name', closing the single syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SUEN' with rounded lips — say English 'seen' but keep the lips pursed from start to finish, so the vowel comes out like French 'su'; one short syllable.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Syn — attested only as the goddess's name, beside the common noun syn, 'denial, refusal', and the verb synja, 'to deny, refuse'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᚢᚾ (s-u-n), the Viking-Age runic rendering — the úr rune ᚢ covers y along with every rounded vowel.

kin.label: The proverb
kin.form: Snorri's orðtak: 'syn er fyrir sett, þá er maðr segir nei' — a denial is set up when a man says no.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: synja, 'to deny, refuse' — the living verb, unbroken from the medieval language.

pronunciation.note: Syn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Old Norse y is a rounded front vowel unknown to English, but the alphabet writes it with an ordinary letter; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Refusal, Defense
domains.subtitle: The Doorkeeper Who Says No
domains.lead: Syn is the eleventh goddess in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur — and the smallest fully grammatical power in the northern pantheon. She guards the door of the hall and shuts it against those who should not enter; at the þing she is appointed to defend the suits she wishes to refute. Her name is the noun itself: syn, 'denial, refusal', and Snorri seals the identity with the proverb the North kept in its mouth — a denial is set up when a man says no. She has no journey, no marriage, no death: her whole mythology is the closed door and the answered accusation, the divine right of refusal.

cards.name: The Hall Door
cards.desc: The door of the hall she keeps and shuts against those who should not enter — the threshold of the divine household made personal, a boundary with a guardian.

cards.name: The Denial
cards.desc: Syn, the noun itself — the word that says no. Snorri's proverb records it: a denial is set up when a man says no, and the goddess is the saying made divine.

cards.name: The Defense at the Þing
cards.desc: At the assembly she is set as defender against the suits she wishes to refute — the lawful no, the answer that stands between an accused person and a false claim.

cards.name: The Eleventh Seat
cards.desc: Her place in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur, counted between Vör and Hlín and declared of no lesser rank than Frigg's company — rank among the goddesses for a single, indispensable function.

symbols.name: The hall door
symbols.meaning: The threshold she holds against those who should not enter — the boundary made personal

symbols.name: The denial (syn)
symbols.meaning: The noun itself, the word that says no — refusal elevated to a divine power

symbols.name: The proverb
symbols.meaning: 'A denial is set up when a man says no' — the goddess remembered in everyday speech, her mythology carried in a saying

symbols.name: The seat among the ásynjur

symbols.name: The defense at the þing

mythology.lead: Syn's dossier is the shortest in the Edda: one sentence in Gylfaginning, one name in the ásynja þulur, one rule in Skáldskaparmál's grammar of kennings. No poem stages her; no saga gives her a second life; no adventure attaches. And yet the tradition never forgot her, because what she guards is not a story but a word — the small, indispensable word 'no' — and Snorri preserves the proverb that proves the North kept both the word and its goddess in daily use.

myths.title: The Eleventh Ásynja
myths.text:
Snorri's catalogue of the goddesses moves from [[frigg|Frigg]] through [[saga|Sága]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gefjon|Gefjon]], [[fulla|Fulla]], [[freyja|Freyja]] and the rest, and arrives at the eleventh: Syn. 'She guards the door of the hall and shuts it against those who should not enter, and she is appointed to defend, at assemblies, the suits she wishes to refute.' Then the sentence that fixes her identity forever: 'hence the proverb that a denial is set up when a man says no.' The catalogue closes with Snotra and Gná, and Snorri adds that these ásynjur are of no lesser rank than the rest.

The whole of her mythology is in that one entry. Two functions are given, and they are one function twice: the doorkeeper who excludes, and the defender who refutes. At the threshold and at the law-court, Syn is the power that keeps the wrong thing out.

myths.title: The Word Made Goddess
myths.text:
Syn's name is not a theonym with a hidden etymology; it is the ordinary noun itself. Old Norse syn means 'denial, refusal'; the verb synja means 'to deny, to refuse', and it saturates the legal prose of the sagas wherever a claim is answered with a no. The lexica connect the word with the family of sannr, 'true' — the denial began as a law term, the truth-speaking by which a false accusation is refused. The goddess of saying no is, at root, the goddess of the truthful answer.

Snorri knows exactly what he is doing when he appends the proverb: he is recording a figure the language itself had already made. Whether Syn was an old goddess whose function shrank to a saying, or an abstraction Snorri's tradition personified on the model of Vör, Hlín and Snotra, the handbooks will not decide; Simek and Lindow class her among the personified functions, and the evidence is too thin to overrule them.

myths.title: The Kenning for a Woman
myths.text:
Skáldskaparmál's rules for the poets keep Syn in the craft of verse: a woman may be periphrased by the name of any ásynja, and Syn stands in the list of goddesses available to the kenning-maker — refusal lending her name to praise, as Baldr's name stands for a warrior and Freyja's for a lady of rank. The ásynja þulur, the versified name-lists preserved with the same section of the Edda, hold her in the catalogue by name.

It is a humble survival, but it is survival: every skald who named a woman after an ásynja worked from a list that included her, and the scribes who copied the þulur kept the doorkeeper's name in the register of the gods long after any cult there may have been was gone.

myths.title: The Silence of the Poems
myths.text:
No eddic poem names Syn. Völuspá's seeress does not number her among the returning gods; Grímnismál's survey of heaven's halls gives her no dwelling; the lays of gods and heroes pass her by entirely. Her whole being rests on Snorri's prose, the þulur, and the noun the whole language spoke. Where [[nanna|Nanna]] at least has her household's halls in verse, Syn has only the sentence — and the saying.

The silence is itself the evidence the handbooks weigh. A figure attested once, in a catalogue, beside a living proverb, is either a genuine minor cult figure the poems happened to miss or a personification the cataloguing mind of the thirteenth century promoted from grammar. The honest record keeps both doors open — which is, perhaps, the one indignity a doorkeeper must bear.

lore.syncretism: Syn's nearest kin are inside her own catalogue: the company of ásynjur whom Snorri lists around her — Vör, 'awareness', who is wise and searching so that nothing can be hidden from her; Hlín, set to guard those whom Frigg wishes to save from danger; Snotra, wise and courteous; Gná, whom Frigg sends on errands through the worlds. Simek and Lindow treat this whole band, Syn among them, as personified functions and abstractions — the grammatically feminine nouns of Old Norse promoted to goddesses, or faded minor deities surviving only as entries in the list. The comparison most often drawn is structural, not borrowed: the doorkeeper type recurs across the North, and the corpus's own great threshold-guardian is Heimdallr at Bifröst — but where Heimdallr watches for what comes, Syn simply refuses it entry. Cross-culturally, nineteenth-century scholars reached for the door-keeping figures of other traditions, even Janus with his gates, but the modern handbooks are cooler: Orchard and Simek note that nothing beyond the single sentence supports reconstruction, and her attestation will not bear the weight. What can be said cleanly is that no other northern goddess is so entirely a speech-act — a goddess whose whole cult, if she ever had one, fits in the space of the word 'no'.
lore.culturalLegacy: Syn's afterlife is the quietest in the pantheon and the most grammatical. The proverb Snorri recorded — a denial is set up when a man says no — remained in circulation as a saying about plain refusal, and the verb synja never died: it lives on in modern Icelandic and Faroese as the ordinary word for denying and refusing, so that the goddess's name is still spoken daily by people who have never heard of her. The handbooks of Norse mythology keep her one-sentence entry with bureaucratic fidelity: Simek, Orchard and Lindow all give her a short article, always the same two functions, always the same scholarly shrug about personification. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities, working through the ásynjur name by name, have found in her a goddess worth invoking for the age of obligations: the patron of boundaries, of the lawful refusal, of the strength to say no at the door and at the judgment-seat — a modern devotion built honestly on the only two functions the sources ever gave her.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Syn is the pantheon's smallest power and perhaps its most modern one. Every other goddess in Snorri's catalogue presides over something the world desires — love, healing, wisdom, safe passage, the keeping of oaths. Syn presides over the thing everyone needs and no one thanks: the refusal. The door that does not open. The claim that does not stand. Hers is the only divine function in the corpus that is purely negative, and the tradition ranks her, deliberately, 'of no lesser worth' — a household is not safe because its doors are beautiful but because someone holds them shut.

And there is a deeper point folded into the etymology. The word she bears is a law term, kin to the word for truth: the denial is not stubbornness but testimony, the truthful no that answers the false claim. In a mythology that ends with the doors of the world broken down at Ragnarǫk, Syn stands at the threshold for as long as the hall stands — the goddess of the boundary, reminding us that a wall is only architecture until someone is willing to say no.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Syn — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᚢᚾ (s-u-n), the úr rune ᚢ covering the rounded front vowel y along with every rounded vowel, so the runic transliteration reads 'sun'. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: syn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 35 (the eleventh ásynja: keeper of the hall door, defender at the þing, and the proverb 'a denial is set up when a man says no'); Skáldskaparmál (women periphrased by the names of the ásynjur) and the ásynja þulur
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. syn, synja; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. syn, synja
de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, s.v. syn, synja (the word's kinship with the family of sannr, 'true'; a law term by origin)
Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, s.v. Syn (attestation confined to Snorri and the þulur; classed among the personified abstractions)

lore.archaeology: Syn is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no place-name preserves her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be identified with her — a silence she shares with most of the minor ásynjur of Snorri's catalogue and one that underwrites the scholarly reading of her as a personified function rather than an independently culted deity. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of Snorri's Edda: the Codex Regius and Codex Wormianus for Gylfaginning 35, and the manuscripts of Skáldskaparmál — including the Codex Regius and AM 748 — for the kenning rule and the ásynja þulur that keep her name in the register of the goddesses. The nearest material context is the word itself: the legal prose of the medieval Icelandic laws and sagas, where synja does its ordinary work of refusing claims, is the closest thing the record offers to a cult site — the door and the þing, preserved on vellum.
